James (and list):

I'm not completely sure this answers your question, but if you consult
the Distance Users Guide, Appendix - MCDS Engine Reference, you will
learn about a Stats file that is created by Distance.  That file can be
accessed, and the global detection function (along with its measures of
uncertainty) can be read by whatever bits and pieces of software you
wish.  Searching the PDF for 'stats file' will reveal great amounts of
detail about this file, its specification, and format.

This engine, named "multiple covariate distance sampling" engine is your
friend for fitting the covariates of interest to you in the detection
function.

messages.body_plain:
Hello Folks,

I am interested in taking a global detection probability function from
program Distance into another program such as SAS or Python and
computing density for each one of my samples (point transects).  Has
anyone ever done this? I would like to incorporate numerous covariates
into the model as well.  I envision it being able to be dynamic such
that the detection probabilities for each of my intervals can be
changed.  Any suggestions would be appreciated!

Thank you.

james martin

mar...@warnell.uga.edu

messages.subject: Finding model selection proportions for model averaging
messages.subject_clean: Finding model selection proportions for model averaging
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,

I am currently using Distance 5.0 Rel 2 to analyse a largish farmland bir=
d
data set obtained through line transects. For some subsets it has turned
out that there exist several different models that would fit the data
about equally well. I am attempting to use model averaging by
bootstrapping to select among those - e.g., 3 different models and 1000
bootstrap runs. What I haven't been able to find out is how to extract
from the results of these runs some indication as to the proportion of
these 1000 runs that were fitted with model 1,2 or 3, respectively. The
bootstrap output file does not seem to contain the relevant information
(maybe I got a bit lost in the format though - according to the
documentation, module #2/statistic #13 would seem to contain what I want
to find out, but the file references no 2-digit statistics codes at all).

Having just read the Buckland et al., June 1997 Biometrics paper, where
this kind of information was fruitfully applied, I'd be grateful if
someone could give me a hint how to extract it from my data!

cheers
florian

---

Centre for the Study of Agriculture, Food and Environment (CSAFE)

messages.subject: Re: Finding model selection proportions for model averaging
messages.subject_clean: Finding model selection proportions for model averaging
messages.body_plain:
Hi Florian (list),

You can tell from current bootstrap stats file output which model was
selected for each run by looking at the 3rd column of numbers
(Estimator) for lines  where the 4th column (Module) is 2.  The number
in the Estimator column tells you which of the estimators you allowed
Distance to choose among was actually chosen.  So, for example, if in
the Model Defintion Properties, Detection function | Estimate tab you
had selected
Half-normal  Cosine
Uniform      Cosine
Half-normal  Hermite polynomial
then bootstrap replicates where the Estimator column has a 1 in it
correspond with the Half-normal/Cosine model, 2 corresponds to the
Uniform/Cosine model and 3 corresponds to the half-normal/Hermite model.
  Hope this makes sense.  Note this is only true when the 4th column
(Module) is 2 -- ie for rows that deal with detection function estimation.

You were looking for Module 2, statistic 13 (key function type).  That
is present in the stats file (the one produced from the original, not
bootstrapped data), along with statistics 14-17 and 101+ (see manual for
details of these).  However, you helped me locate a bug where these are
not produced in the bootstrap stats file.  I have now fixed that bug, so
all of these statistics are now produced for each bootstrap replicate.
If you want an updated copy of the mcds analysis engine, mcds.exe then

messages.subject: Re: Finding model selection proportions for model averaging
messages.subject_clean: Finding model selection proportions for model averaging
messages.body_plain:
Hi Florian (list),

You can tell from current bootstrap stats file output which model was
selected for each run by looking at the 3rd column of numbers
(Estimator) for lines  where the 4th column (Module) is 2.  The number
in the Estimator column tells you which of the estimators you allowed
Distance to choose among was actually chosen.  So, for example, if in
the Model Defintion Properties, Detection function | Estimate tab you
had selected
Half-normal  Cosine
Uniform      Cosine
Half-normal  Hermite polynomial
then bootstrap replicates where the Estimator column has a 1 in it
correspond with the Half-normal/Cosine model, 2 corresponds to the
Uniform/Cosine model and 3 corresponds to the half-normal/Hermite model.
  Hope this makes sense.  Note this is only true when the 4th column
(Module) is 2 -- ie for rows that deal with detection function estimation.

You were looking for Module 2, statistic 13 (key function type).  That
is present in the stats file (the one produced from the original, not
bootstrapped data), along with statistics 14-17 and 101+ (see manual for
details of these).  However, you helped me locate a bug where these are
not produced in the bootstrap stats file.  I have now fixed that bug, so
all of these statistics are now produced for each bootstrap replicate.
If you want an updated copy of the mcds analysis engine, mcds.exe then
email me off the list.  The fix will be generally available in the next
release of Distance.

messages.subject: Post-stratification by time or time as a covariate?
messages.subject_clean: Post-stratification by time or time as a covariate?
messages.body_plain:
Hello list,

I am looking for some guidance on how to treat a time factor for a projec=
t
that involved repeat visits (with different line transects each time) to =
a
series of sites.
Background: I carried out bird surveys on 12 farms, arranged into 4 farm
clusters, with 10 repeat visits of 10 line transects each. The repeat
visits were spread over 2 years. I am chiefly interested in finding
cluster- and farm-level density estimates that are averaged over the
entire time period.

It seems that the two methods of accounting for the fact that the data
comes in 10 sets of 10-transect repeat visits each rather than 100
transects per farm at the same time (i.e. accounting for seasonal
variations in detectability), would be a) post-stratification by time
period, or b) adding time period as a covariate. I am not sure how
equivalent these methods would be. Specifically, I would like to avoid
having time period in the post-stratification slot, as practically any
analysis I run would need it there, and I thus would be unable to
post-stratify by any other factor of interest (e.g. geographic strata,
observer, sex). Including it as a covariate would leave me a lot more roo=
m
for customizing the analyses for other foci, but would the effect be
equivalent? I can't really come to a conclusion on that from the
documentation, and would value any input!

cheers
florian

--=20
